newsitem.title: INDIA: Morgan Stanley says Moody's too harsh on India.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley says Moody's too harsh on India.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Morgan Stanley issued a "message of confidence" in India's economy on Tuesday and called a controversial assessment by U.S. credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service unduly harsh.

A Morgan Stanley credit report gave Indian corporate debt a "buy" rating, saying a six-year-old economic reform programme had pushed up economic growth to seven percent last year while inflation had come down.
It took issue with a credit rating earlier this month by Moody's which provoked strong criticism from a range of Indian political parties.

Moody's said India's unstable political environment, directionless economic policies and a deterioration in its macroeconomic balances had led it to take an unfavourable outlook on the nation's sovereign rating.
"In our view, this is an unduly harsh assessment of the country's creditworthiness," Morgan Stanley sovereign credit analyst Robert Smalley said in the report.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram had earlier taken issue with the Moody's assessment.
"I think Moody's rating's wrong. I mean whoever gave them the inputs must have given it to them at least four months ago," Chidambaram told Reuters in an interview last weekend.
Morgan Stanley said it agreed with Chidambaram that Moody's had not taken into account the government's proposed budget for 1997/98, which begins on April 1.
The budget's cornerstone is tax rate cuts to stimulate the economy. "This budget is a pro-growth, pro-business package," Morgan Stanley said.

The investment bank said the budget's assumption that gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by at least seven percent in 1997/98 and the fiscal deficit would fall to 4.5 percent of GDP from 5.0 percent this year were somewhat aggressive but achievable.

"With this budget the current government has laid out a plan to increase confidence and to spur growth -- not the stuff of a 'directionless' economic policy, as Moody's would have us believe," Morgan Stanley said.
Still, Morgan Stanley said it was important for India to press ahead with reforms by privatising state-owned firms and opening the financial sector to outside competition.

Morgan Stanley said it believed U.S. credit rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp would look to upgrade India to BBB- from BB+ in the next 12 to 18 months. "We view the Republic of India as a stable low BBB credit," Smalley said.
BBB is an investment grade rating reflecting a perceived low expectation of risk. BB is a speculative rating indicating a possibility of investment risk developing.
Morgan Stanley said it had more than $1.2 billion in assets under custody in India and had helped a large number of Indian corporations raise money in global markets.

It helped float India's first global depositary receipt (GDR) equity offering in 1992, and is one of the co-managers for a $570 million GDR issue by India's state-run overseas telecommunications monopoly Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL), expected to be launched soon.
